title: HUD's FHA Crackdown Shuts Out Visa Holders as Home Loans Fall to Near Zero
excerpt: Non-permanent residents went from 5.8% of FHA purchase originations to 0.1% after the May 2025 rule change — and conventional lending has not picked up the slack.
body:
• Federal Housing Administration mortgages for non-permanent residents have collapsed from 5.8% of FHA purchase originations to about 0.1%, according to origination data from Intercontinental Exchange — effectively the zero the Trump administration intended.
  • The cause: HUD's March 26, 2025 Mortgagee Letter 2025-09, which stripped the "non-permanent resident" category from FHA programs effective May 25, 2025 — shutting out H-1B holders, OPT students, many DACA recipients, and pending-asylum applicants.
  • If you're on an H-1B or other work visa and house-hunting: the FHA route (with its 3.5% minimum down payment) is closed. Conventional loans through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac still accept lawful non-permanent residents — but expect to need stronger credit and larger down payments; non-QM loans are a pricier fallback. Existing FHA loans are unaffected.
  • The hit is worst in tech and Sun Belt markets: Salt Lake City went from 26% of FHA purchases to non-permanent residents to 0.15%; San Jose from 10% to zero; Orlando from 16.1% to 0.2%.

The Number HUD Wanted to Hit: Zero

The Department of Housing and Urban Development announced Friday that government-backed home loans for non-permanent residents have fallen to nearly zero — and treated it as a victory. "President Trump promised to put Americans first, and HUD delivered," Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. "We are preventing illegals and non-residents from accessing taxpayer-backed programs at the expense of American homebuyers. Today, that share is zero."

https://x.com/GuntherEagleman/status/2108558349696749753

The data backs the boast. Origination data from Intercontinental Exchange, shared with HousingWire, shows non-permanent residents accounted for 5.8% of FHA purchase originations before the policy change — and about 0.1% after. Across all loan types, their share of purchase mortgages fell 2.2 percentage points to 3.4%. A separate analysis by researchers at JBREC found non-permanent residents (NPRs) accounted for less than 1% of FHA-backed loans in June, dropping to nearly zero in July and August — the lowest level in a data series stretching back to February 2018.

How the Door Closed

On March 26, 2025, HUD issued Mortgagee Letter 2025-09 and Title I Letter 490, removing the "non-permanent resident" category from FHA's Single Family Title I and Title II programs, effective for loans with case numbers assigned on or after May 25, 2025. Overnight, the FHA Handbook sections that had let lawfully present non-citizens with work authorization qualify — H-1B holders, OPT students, some DACA recipients, people with pending asylum claims — were gone. A Social Security number alone no longer proves eligibility; lenders must now verify citizenship or permanent residency. Only US citizens, lawful permanent residents, and certain nationals of Compact of Free Association countries remain eligible. Existing FHA loans were left untouched, and applications with case numbers before the cutoff proceeded under the old rules.

The timing produced a stampede: JBREC's Alex Thomas told Newsweek there was "a clear surge in FHA loan locks by non-permanent residents in April and May, when NPR borrowers rushed to lock in their loan before the new rule took effect." Then the cliff. "Policy shifts in housing finance often show up quickly in the data," Thomas said — and this one did.

The Markets That Felt It Most

The pain is concentrated where visa-holding professionals cluster. In Salt Lake City, non-permanent residents made up 26% of FHA purchase originations before the rule; afterward, 0.15%. Provo fell from 20% to under 0.5%. Florida markets cratered: Orlando from 16.1% to 0.2%, Lakeland from 13.6% to 0.16%, Cape Coral and Miami from 10% to under 1%. Raleigh dropped from 11.1% to 0.8%. And San Jose — the capital of H-1B America — went from about 10% to zero.

Conventional lending has not picked up the slack. ICE data shows non-permanent resident volume in conventional prime conforming loans stayed roughly flat rather than rising to offset the FHA decline — suggesting many would-be buyers simply stopped buying, a finding echoed by JBREC's Thomas, who attributed the plunge primarily to borrowers exiting the market.

"I am currently working on a loan in one such scenario, and it does make it far more difficult for the borrower to qualify. For better or for worse, that was the main desired result of the policy change."

— Isaac Schultz, home loan specialist, Churchill Mortgage

The remaining options are conventional loans — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac still permit lawful non-permanent residents — and non-QM products, both with stricter terms. "Some of these non-permanent residents will end up having to put more money down, work on improving their credit scores to qualify, or simply will need to wait until they obtain permanent-resident status," said Michael Brown, a Tennessee-based loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage.

Part of a Larger Squeeze

The FHA rule is one front in a multi-front campaign. It followed the reversal of a Biden-era policy that had extended FHA eligibility to DACA recipients — a move three House Democrats (Pete Aguilar, Juan Vargas, and Sylvia Garcia) are now trying to undo with the Housing Stability for Dreamers Act. And it lands alongside last month's presidential proclamation imposing a $100,000 application fee on new H-1B visas. "The FHA's May restriction on lending to H-1B visa holders and other non-permanent residents is putting pressure on entry-level home-buying in some key housing markets already dealing with weak sales & too much supply," one JBREC researcher noted.

For a program that has long been the entry ramp to American homeownership — NPRs made up about 4% of FHA volume nationally in 2024, historically 2-3% — the exclusion raises a question beyond housing: whether the cumulative cost of working in America, from visa fees to denied mortgages, is starting to change where the world's skilled professionals choose to go.
